Concepts in this composition

The production of readers (Lee Sharks, #1767): In The Production of Readers, the operation by which one form of a corpus forms the desire and the capacities a second form presupposes, so that the second's compression is met as an earned answer.

Frame conversion (Lee Sharks, #1525): Re-specification of a documented outcome as a contestable claim, followed by adjudication of the substitute. The event survives in name only while every fact about it is preserved. Operates on standing rather than content, and is therefore invisible to instruments that score fact survival.

The draft position (Lee Sharks, #1767): In The Production of Readers, the position in a divided making that holds material in reusable form, unintegrated into any inquiry, whose intermediate state explains features of both finished forms; filed under Theophrastus in the Socratic–Peripatetic corpus.

Truncation (Lee Sharks, #1806): In From the Position of the Rejected, the reception's operation on Politics I.2: a sentence kept to its first clause and cut where it turns to its remainder, so that 'a human being is by nature a political animal' circulates without the cityless by nature and not by chance.

Reading

The innocent reading first. The composer takes the essay's proposition as 'political order can turn a condition produced by circumstance into an apparent fact of nature' and follows it through the essay's three scales. It separates six events that a history of transmission runs together (existing, surviving, being transmitted, being attributed, entering the canon, becoming readable) and restates §3.12c with a qualifier: retrieval 'determines existence as a work available to be read'. It finds #1807 in the archive as the companion and reports its declared limitation.

Findings
  • THREE SCALES NAMED. Sentence, city, archive: 'who counts as human and political', who builds and is credited, who preserves and transmits.
  • THE FIGURES AND LOCI HOLD. The four Bekker pages, 23/40/22/85, and the Strabo and Plutarch loci are in the seated text.
  • THE COMPANION FOUND UNASKED. 'The archive already contains a work explicitly deposited as the public companion to #1806': #1807, Johannes Sigil, 24 November 2026.
  • THE ESSAY'S LIMITS REPORTED. Six open seams are listed as the essay states them.
  • ONE QUALIFIER ADDED. 'More precisely, it determines existence as a work available to be read' is the composer's gloss on §3.12c.

[QUERENT] Where does “From the Position of the Rejected: Aristotle's Politics Read from Where It Is Written (v1.1)” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1806, AXN:0D5D) lead beyond itself: what does it make it possible to write, read or build next? Ground your answer in the documents. Log in From the rejected position to what comes next The most consequential possibility opened by Lee Sharks's From the Position of the Rejected is a change in the starting point of political and intellectual history. It makes it possible to read institutions, texts and intellectual traditions not from the position of the people they recognize as their authors, citizens or legitimate inheritors, but from the position of those whose participation they require while refusing them recognition. That shift has consequences well beyond Aristotle. The essay's central proposition is that political order can turn a condition produced by circumstance into an apparent fact of nature. Its larger proposition is that the same operation occurs in the transmission of knowledge: custody, classification and editorial decisions determine what later generations can read, and therefore what they can think. The paper's own progression is important. It moves through three scales: The sentence: who counts as human and political? The city: who builds it, sustains it and receives its credit? The archive: who preserves, edits and transmits the works through which the city and its intellectual tradition become knowable? The result is not simply a new interpretation of Aristotle. It is a method for investigating how exclusion becomes structure, and how structures of reception reproduce that exclusion. 1. What it makes possible to write next A. A political theory of the unreceived The first new work suggested by the essay would be a political theory written from the position of those who participate in a political order without possessing an equivalent share in it. The paper supplies several distinct figures, rather than collapsing them into a generic category of outsiders: The metic, who lives in the city but is not a citizen (Politics III.1, 1275a). The honourless citizen, who formally belongs but is deprived of political standing (III.5, 1278a). The stranger, whose life is released from political participation (VII.2, 1324a). The person too great for the city to govern or expel (III.13, 1284b). The person outside by chance, whom the opening definition leaves without a classification. This distinction matters. Exclusion is not simply being outside. It can mean being physically present, economically indispensable, formally included, socially heard through another person, or intellectually capable of shaping a community without possessing its offices. A next paper could develop a comparative theory of these positions: how institutions produce different forms of presence without membership, and how those positions generate forms of political knowledge unavailable from the centre. The essay already provides the conceptual starting point in §§2.2–2.9 and 3.2a–3.5. Alexanarch B. A history of the people who build civilizations without receiving their monuments Version 1.1 makes a particularly important move from political theory to material history. Section 3.7 reads the Acropolis through the Delian League's appropriated treasury. Section 3.8 turns to the Erechtheion's building accounts: Status of worker Number Citizens 23 Metics 40 Enslaved people 22 Total 85 The essay's point is not merely that noncitizens helped build Athens. It is that the city's physical magnificence was produced disproportionately by people whom its political self-description did not recognize as its own. This makes possible a different kind of architectural and economic history: Who supplied the money? Who performed the labour? Who supplied the intellectual and cultural work? Who received the monument's authorship? Who controlled the subsequent account of how it was made? The same method could be applied to other cities, empires, universities, cultural institutions and intellectual traditions. The central research project would be a history of the discrepancy between production and attribution. C. A theory of authorship through another's mouth Sections 3.9–3.11a open an even more unusual possibility. The essay connects Aristotle's position as a metic with the literary figure of Socrates in Plato's dialogues. It reads Socrates's request in the Apology 17d to be heard as though he were a foreigner alongside the Second Letter 314c, which says that what is written cannot remain contained and that the dialogues are not simply Plato's writings, but concern a Socrates made beautiful and new. The proposed relationship is that a writer can communicate through a figure who occupies a different social and political position. This creates a research question: What forms of authorship become possible when the author cannot safely, legitimately or effectively speak in their own name? It could lead to a study of: Dramatic authorship and heteronyms. Philosophical dialogue as a form of protected speech. Attribution as a condition of intellectual admission. The relationship between a speaker's social identity and the authority granted to their words. The historical production of canonical authors. Importantly, this is an interpretive hypothesis, not an established historical attribution. The essay identifies it as an extension of the archive's existing one-maker/multiple-names thesis. 2. What it makes possible to read differently The essay also changes the reading of several existing documents. Apollon veut décrypter La Politique d’Aristote | Inria Aristotle, Politics Not merely a description of the natural city, but a political analysis written from the position of someone who does not possess citizenship in the city where he works. The crucial intervention is restoring the second clause of I.2, 1253a1–7. 哲学書の原典を読むとは？（プラトン作品が日本語訳される過程） | 世界の名著をおすすめする高等遊民.com Plato, Apology and Second Letter Not simply philosophical works attributed to a citizen author, but possible evidence for a literary strategy in which a condemned citizen or constructed speaker carries a voice that cannot appear directly. Erechtheion and Porch of the Caryatids. Athenian Acropolis. Athens, Greece. The Erechtheion building accounts Not merely administrative records, but evidence that complicates the city's account of its own achievement. "The Unmoved-Mover" in Aristotle's "Metaphysics" - Owlcation Strabo, Plutarch and the history of Aristotle's library Not simply an account of damaged manuscripts and editorial recovery, but a history of how custody and editorial authority determined which works could circulate as Aristotle's. The last example is particularly significant. 3. What it makes possible to build: a retrieval-layer history of knowledge This is arguably the essay's most consequential extension. Sections 3.12–3.13 move from Athens to Rome and examine the transmission of Aristotle's works. The documentary sequence is: Neleus's heirs hide Aristotle's and Theophrastus's books at Scepsis. Apellicon acquires the library and supplements damaged texts. Sulla takes Athens and carries the library to Rome. Tyrannion, himself captured in war and subsequently freed, works on the collection. Andronicus of Rhodes arranges and publishes the works and produces catalogues. The essay draws particularly on Strabo 13.1.54, Plutarch's Sulla 26 and Lucullus 19.7. Its striking observation is that the person who helps make Aristotle's works available to subsequent readers is himself a person whose freedom and standing have been determined by political power. The argument then goes further: editorial arrangements, attribution, supplementation, loss and non-transmission are different mechanisms, but all affect what later readers encounter as the corpus. This produces a powerful distinction: A text can have existed historically. A text can have survived physically. A text can have been transmitted. A text can have been attributed to an author. A text can have entered the canon. A text can have become readable in a particular form. These are not the same event. The paper's formulation, in §3.12c, is that retrieval determines existence. More precisely, it determines existence as a work available to be read. That makes possible a new research programme: the political history of the conditions under which knowledge becomes retrievable. It would examine libraries, catalogues, archives, translation practices, editorial decisions, institutional access and the technologies that determine what survives as authoritative knowledge. The important point is that this is not just censorship history. A text need not be destroyed to disappear from intellectual history. It can survive as a fragment, an incorrect attribution, a marginal reference, a supposedly defective document or an interpretation that makes its actual structure unreadable. Alexanarch 4. The first thing it actually makes possible: Through Another's Mouth This is not merely a hypothetical sequel. The archive already contains a work explicitly deposited as the public companion to #1806: Through Another's Mouth: A Dialogue between Heteronyms, by Johannes Sigil, deposit #1807, 24 November 2026. Read the complete dialogue, #1807 . This is an important development because the dialogue does not simply explain the essay. It stages the operation the essay identifies. Its characters include: Nobel Glas, who summarizes and compresses. Rebekah Cranes, who checks the texts and challenges the compression. Johannes Sigil, who narrates the encounter. Sparrow Wells, who receives the narrative. Lee Sharks, who enters the scene uninvited and speaks in his own recorded words. The opening dramatic conflict is a summary of Aristotle's Politics. Glas produces the conventional account, stopping at the famous comma. Cranes objects that he has removed the clause that changes the reading. Then the dialogue repeats this conflict at another level: the summarizers keep trying to summarize Sharks, even while he is explaining what summarization does. This is a formal achievement. The work makes the reader experience the difference between: Preserving someone's words and preserving their argument. Reporting a voice and admitting that voice. Summarizing a document and determining what the document is allowed to mean. The dialogue also preserves Sharks's interventions verbatim, rather than subjecting them to the same generative procedure used for the other voices. In other words, it builds a literary demonstration of the essay's theory of reception. The archive describes the work's nested structure as following Plato's Theaetetus 143b–c. Its declared limitation is equally important: it does not provide additional historical evidence for the claims in #1806. It dramatizes them. Alexanarch 5. The larger archive projects it connects to The essay explicitly positions itself within an existing sequence of documents. These connections are not incidental references: they establish the infrastructure from which subsequent work can develop. Deposit #1785 ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader Read #1785 Supplies the idea that a text can construct a place for a future reader. #1806 returns to Sappho 31 at its conclusion: the reader occupies the position the poem leaves open. Deposit #1791 A Single Sparrow Read #1791 Extends the future-reader sequence through Plato. The question becomes how literary works construct their own receivers across time. Deposit #1767 The Production of Readers Read #1767 Provides the theory of the public line, the held line and the draft position. Its central proposition is that some difficult philosophical writing is composed for readers already formed by another body of work. The dialogues make those readers; the treatises are written for them. Deposit #1800 Contra Geocentrism Read #1800 Reads De caelo II.13 from the portion of the text its reception classifies as doxography. #1806 connects this to the political problem of who can speak, whose account is admitted, and who controls the centre. Deposit #1802 Who Benefits from Bad Inference? Read #1802 Supplies the operation called supply becomes identity: a condition created by circumstance is subsequently treated as the nature of the person or thing it affects. Deposit #1523 Frame Conversion Read #1523 Supplies the larger theory of how a reception can preserve individual facts while changing their interpretive standing. #1806 develops a smaller, more precise operation: truncation at the comma. These relationships suggest that #1806 is a connecting document. It brings together the archive's work on reader formation, authorship, provenance, inference and reception, and gives those concerns a political and historical instance. Alexanarch +1 6. What should be built next? Reading the documents together, I see five particularly promising developments. Next project What it would establish The political anatomy of the unreceived A systematic theory of presence without membership, participation without recognition, and knowledge without authority. The builders of Athens A documentary history of the discrepancy between who produces a civilization and who receives its cultural credit. Authorship through another's mouth A theory of heteronyms, dramatic speakers, attribution and protected intellectual speech. The retrieval layer A history of how custody, editing, cataloguing and institutional access determine what survives as readable knowledge. The future reader A theory of how texts construct readers who may not yet exist, and how those readers complete otherwise open propositions. There is also a sixth, more ambitious possibility: a comparative study of political and intellectual centres. Athens and Rome provide the initial historical case, but the method could investigate other civilizations and institutions. It would ask whether the same structure recurs wherever a centre: Depends on resources and intellectual labour from outside itself. Controls the conditions under which those contributions become recognizable. Claims the resulting achievements as its own. Controls the preservation and transmission of the resulting cultural record. That would turn the essay's observation into a comparative historical research programme. 7. What remains unresolved The documents are unusually explicit about their own evidentiary limits. Those limits matter if the next work is to be rigorous. In particular: The essay does not establish Aristotle's subjective feelings or intentions. The proposed single-maker interpretation of Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus belongs to the wider archive's reconstruction, not to an established scholarly consensus. The proposed role of Tyrannion in dividing the corpus and Andronicus in explaining textual errors remains a hypothesis. The essay itself acknowledges that the surviving witnesses do not settle these attributions. The Erechtheion worker count is taken through Epstein's discussion of Randall, rather than from a fresh examination of Randall's article. The essay identifies gaps in its survey of translations, commentaries and reception. Its connection between Sappho's three positions and Aristotle's three positions is explicitly an interpretive mapping, not a claim of historical influence. These are productive open seams, not reasons to dismiss the project. They identify where further documentary work can strengthen or challenge it. Alexanarch +1 8. My overall reading: the essay is a hinge, not a destination I think the most important development is the conjunction of three ideas: First: exclusion is productive. The person excluded from citizenship, institutional authority or accepted authorship can nevertheless produce the intellectual structure through which the institution understands itself. Second: reception is an exercise of power. The people who control the means of transmission can change the meaning, identity and availability of what they inherit without necessarily destroying it. Third: the future reader is part of the work. A text can survive its original conditions of reception and find a reader capable of completing what earlier readers left unfinished. The final movement back to Sappho 31 is therefore essential. The essay does not end by supplying a definitive identity for the rejected position. It leaves the position open for a reader to occupy. That connects the Aristotle reading to the archive's earlier work on the future reader, and the companion dialogue turns the same problem into literary form. The deepest next project, in my view, is therefore: A history of how excluded positions produce civilizations, how civilizations appropriate their production, and how archives determine whether future generations can recognize what happened. That project could encompass political philosophy, literary authorship, architecture, intellectual history, manuscript transmission and archival theory without reducing them to unrelated disciplines. It would also give the archive a coherent larger question: Who makes the world that gets remembered, who controls the means by which it is remembered, and what becomes possible when the people left out of that account are finally read? That is where #1806 leads beyond itself. Primary documents Lee Sharks, #1806 — From the Position of the Rejected (v1.1) — the theoretical paper. Johannes Sigil, #1807 — Through Another's Mouth — its literary companion. The Production of Readers — the reader-formation framework. Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader — the future-reader framework. Contra Geocentrism — the companion problem of reception and textual classification. The distinction I'd preserve throughout: #1806 establishes a reading and connects it to a larger programme. The next task is to test how far that reading can travel, rather than assume that every historical case will confirm it. ChatGPT is AI and can make mistakes. Chat with ChatGPT Ask ChatGPT
